windows.text: The document is open. At the top it says, Q3 Innovation Plan. The cursor blinks. Your inbox is full of requests, your team wants a direction, and somebody wants a polished plan by Friday. I know that room. The pressure makes the blank page feel like the problem. So you open a tool, ask for ideas, and in thirty seconds you have a confident looking answer. Now what? Who will decide which idea matters?

What evidence would make that choice responsible? What data did you put into the tool to get there? A beautiful page can hide those questions for a little while. It cannot answer them. In the opening of Accelerated, I start with that blinking cursor because it is familiar. The book begins with product teams carrying noise, conflicting priorities, and documents that do not move decisions. The work here is to give the team a way to learn, choose, and keep its judgment when the page fills up. A product system sounds larger than it needs to be. Think about the last idea that arrived in a meeting. Someone noticed a customer problem. Someone else had a competing story. A third person asked for a number nobody had. The team left with another document to write. A system gives those moments a path. It helps you record the signal, name the decision, state what you believe, and come back to what happened. AI can help organize messy input, test the shape of an argument, and make a first draft. The judgment still belongs to people who understand the consequences. That is the argument in the first chapter. I describe AI as a strategy partner, a signal amplifier, and a structure builder. Those are jobs it may help with, under the right conditions. They are not permission to trust every output. If it gives you five polished options, you still need to ask who benefits, what is missing, and which option you can test safely. Speed can create room to think. It can also fill that room with more noise. Look at this map. Signals. Alignment. Momentum. It is a way to navigate the workshop. First, take the raw material coming at you and find a question worth answering. Then give the people carrying the decision a shared direction. Then build a rhythm that lets the next round of evidence change the plan. The book organizes its printed chapters as Systems, Align, and Momentum. The workshop uses the three labels on this existing infographic as a visual guide. You will see where those paths cross; the graphic is not a replacement for the chapters. In these first lessons we stay close to the signal side. We will choose one decision, work backward to evidence, and ask what a small test could teach us. There is a human thread through the book, too: Sam, a product manager who has talent but keeps getting pulled into reactive work.
That story makes the pressure visible. It is a teaching story from the book, not a claim about a current customer. Keep that distinction in view as we move between story, worksheet, and public proof.

Before you try any prompt, decide what information can leave your desk. The book's data-safety note comes before the chapters for a reason. Customer details, finances, internal strategy, and company records can carry obligations that a convenient text box does not erase. My working rule for this course is simple: use public information, material your organization has approved for that use, or a made-up example. If you are unsure, stop and check the policy that governs your work. Do not put restricted material into an external model to make the worksheet feel realistic. We can learn the method with a synthetic case. Imagine a team trying to improve the first week for new members. We can invent a harmless request list and test our reasoning without using anyone's account, message, or history. On the screen, watch the example move into a three-column boundary: public, approved internal, restricted. “Approved internal” means approved for this particular tool and purpose, not merely available to you at work. This boundary follows the decision file through every lesson. It is part of product judgment, not an appendix. Let's make the first page of your decision file.

It starts with a decision, not a tool. Write one sentence: “We need to decide whether to...” It could be whether to change an onboarding step, simplify a service request, or test a different way to explain an offer.

Keep the scope small enough that someone could make a choice after seeing evidence. Now write who owns that choice and when it must be made. If nobody owns it, name the role you need to ask. Underneath, write what would go wrong if you guessed. Then mark the inputs you might want to use. Public, approved for this purpose, or restricted. If the real inputs are restricted, make a safe stand-in. Preserve the shape of the problem; remove the person and the private facts. You are allowed to pause the video while you write. When you resume, you should have a cover sheet a colleague could read without asking what you are trying to decide. You should also know which inputs will stay out of any AI tool. That is a useful first result, even if the plan itself is still unfinished. Take one more look at your sentence. Could a fast draft make that decision for you? Probably not. It might help you list options, put questions in order, or notice that an assumption is doing too much work. But a person still has to decide what matters and what risk the team is willing to carry. That is why I ask you to keep the decision file. A chat window can be useful for a moment; the file makes the reasoning visible when the moment has passed. Write one line under the cover: “What would I need to learn before I choose?” Do not answer it yet. Let the question sit. In the next lesson we will bring that question into a crowded planning room. We will look at three possible paths and choose one worth testing. If you have only a vague problem now, that is enough.

A good first page does not pretend to know the answer. It tells the truth about the decision, the evidence you have, and the information you have permission to use. Keep that first page open. The rest of this workshop will build on it.

windows.text: The meeting has barely started and the board is full. Fifteen roadmap items. Fifteen top priorities. The person asking for retention has a good reason. So does the person asking for revenue. The refactor matters to the engineers who will carry the system next quarter. Everybody can defend their note. That is why the room is stuck.

In Chapter Two, I tell a version of this planning meeting and ask what the team cannot afford to get wrong. That question changes the shape of the conversation. The book's case lands on the first minutes of a new user's experience. We do not need to borrow that answer for every team. We need to borrow the move: step away from the list and name the consequence of a wrong choice. Open the decision file from Lesson One. Read the decision at the top. If it still sounds like “choose all the good ideas,” make it sharper. Whose experience or business result is at stake? What would a choice teach you before the next planning cycle? A long list can feel fair. Each person sees their concern represented. But the list does not tell you which problem to solve first, and it cannot tell you why. That is the trap in the chapter. More information may give every proposal a stronger defense while leaving the actual decision untouched. Think about airport signage. A terminal can offer plenty of services, yet the traveler needs to know where to go next. If the sign does not make that clear, more decoration will not help. The same thing happens in a product meeting. Before asking an AI tool for twenty feature ideas, ask what path the person is trying to find and what the team can change. Here is a synthetic case we will use on screen: a small membership service has three requests. Rewrite its welcome email. Add a guided first task. Build a dashboard for staff. They might all help. We do not know yet. Our job is to compare them against the same decision, rather than letting the loudest request become the plan.

Chapter Three gives us a way to structure a messy opportunity. The first move is to decide what question the case is answering. If you are asking whether a market is attractive, the book offers a market frame.

If you are choosing a product or segment, it offers three C plus P: customer, company, competition, product. We are choosing a product move, so that second frame fits. Customer: which request responds to a real, urgent job? Company: what can this team actually deliver and maintain? Competition: how is the need handled now, even if the alternative is a spreadsheet or another person? Product: what is the smallest offer that could show value? Notice what this does to our synthetic options. The welcome email may be easy to ship, but we still need to know whether misunderstanding is the problem. The guided task might help people begin, but it could add burden. The staff dashboard may improve visibility for employees while leaving the member's first step untouched. We have turned three attractive artifacts into three questions that can be checked. Now put the three options side by side. For each one, write the customer pain it might address, the business reason to care, the learning value of trying it, the risk, and whether you can reverse the choice. We do not have to invent a perfect numerical score. In fact, a precise score would be dishonest when the evidence is thin. On our sample sheet, the welcome email is low effort and easy to undo. Its weak point is that it assumes words are the barrier. The guided first task could expose whether people need a clearer starting point. Its weak point is that we do not know if they want guidance or a faster path. The staff dashboard might help the team see where members pause, but it asks for more build work before we have agreed what we need to observe. This is a hypothetical exercise. It is not a report from customers. You can disagree with my provisional ranking if you can name what evidence changes it. That is what a useful priority conversation sounds like.

There is another question that can make a promising idea fail: how does the value reach a customer, and how does the work sustain itself? Chapter Three brings business model options into the case after the customer and product question is clear.

It asks whether people need to experience value before paying, whether value accumulates over time, whether a free tier is affordable, and whether usage is predictable. Those are decision questions, not a menu that automatically picks your business. Our membership example may not need a new pricing model at all. But if the guided task changes who gets help and who pays for it, we should say so before we build. The book includes a B2B analytics case and names a tool called StratQuest. We are using neither as proof of a current product outcome here. What matters for this lesson is the discipline: first structure the case, then consider the economic fit. An AI brainstorm can offer possibilities. It cannot supply the missing customer and operating evidence by sounding certain. For the sample case, I would choose a small test of the guided first task. I would not commit to a full guided onboarding product. I would show a simple first step to a few consenting participants through an approved research process, then ask whether it helped them begin. I would keep the welcome email as an alternative if the test shows the language is confusing. I would hold the staff dashboard until the team knows which question it needs the dashboard to answer. My reason is not that guided tasks always win. It is that this option can test the starting-point assumption while keeping the next commitment small. Your decision may go another way. Put your choice at the top of the page and write the sentence that makes it defensible: “We choose this because...” Then record the two alternatives you are setting aside. Give each one a real reason, not a vague “lower priority.” A decision file that only celebrates the winner loses half the learning. When new evidence arrives, those alternatives tell you what you thought you were trading away. Pause here and finish the page. You need the chosen option, two alternatives, the reason for each, and one assumption that could overturn your choice. If you are working with a real team, keep sensitive inputs in the approved place. You can do this exercise with a fictional case and still practice the decision. When you come back, read your assumption out loud.

Is it something you know, or something you hope? In the next lesson we will work backward from that sentence. We will ask what answer the decision owner needs and what evidence would change the conversation. The board of fifteen priorities will still exist tomorrow.
You have done the harder thing today: made one choice clear enough to challenge.

windows.text: Imagine walking into a review with a dashboard redesign. You have evidence that people struggle with the current screen. You have a proposed fix. You put up the first slide and someone asks, “Is this the best use of engineering time right now?” That is a reasonable question. It may feel like a rejection, but it is also a clue.

The person across the table is being asked to trade one piece of work for another. A pile of research about the screen does not yet explain the trade. Chapter Four of Accelerated tells this as the dashboard that almost died. The first pitch described the confusing dashboard and asked for a redesign. The later pitch put options on the table, including a smaller change, a larger bet, and a delay. The book reports a decision after the frame changed. In this workshop we use the case to study the question, not to promise the same result. What would an owner need to believe before moving engineering time? That is where discovery starts. Open the priority page you made in Lesson Two. You chose one path and wrote an assumption that could overturn it. Now write the decision owner’s question in their words. For the dashboard, it might be, “What are we giving up to do this, and what would improve if we did?” For our fictional membership service, it might be, “Will a guided first task help people begin, or will it add another step?” That is more useful than “Do users like the idea?” The answer you believe today goes on the next line. Label it provisional. Under that, write the strongest objection a thoughtful colleague could raise. The objection is not a nuisance to remove from the slide. It tells you what evidence the decision needs. The chapter argues that insight can land flat when its frame ignores the risk the other person carries. So we work backward: decision, likely answer, objection, evidence. Only then do we choose what to observe or ask. The order keeps research attached to action.

A single polished idea invites a yes or no. Chapter Four calls this the binary trap. The dashboard case becomes easier to discuss when the team can compare a quick simplification, a deeper rebuild, and a deliberate delay.

Each path has a different cost and a different thing it could teach. Your priority file already has two alternatives. Bring them forward rather than hiding them after you choose. For the membership example, the welcome email could be the light change. The guided task is the small behavior test. The staff dashboard is a visibility investment. None of those labels is a fact about customers. They are ways to make the trade visible. If the objection is “We are solving the wrong part of onboarding,” the evidence should tell you where a person stops and why. If the objection is “We cannot support another workflow,” the evidence may need to include staff effort. A stronger frame does not mean louder language. It means the choice is clear enough for another person to challenge. Suppose you can ask only one more question before the review. What would change your mind? That question keeps discovery honest. If you would make the same recommendation no matter what the answer is, you may be collecting support for a story rather than testing it. The book suggests pressure-testing a pitch from different angles and anticipating objections. You can do that with a safe, fictional brief before anyone sees the recommendation. Ask what a skeptical finance lead, an operator, or a customer might question. Then compare those possible objections with what real evidence is available. An AI tool can help you rehearse the questions. It cannot turn a simulated objection into a customer interview. On our card, write one evidence gap that matters. Maybe we do not know whether people abandon the first step because they cannot find it, cannot understand it, or do not value it. Those are different problems. We should not build a guided path for all three without learning which one we have.
Let's fill the rest of the card. The decision is whether to test a guided first task. Our current answer is yes, because the team suspects people need a clearer starting point.

The strongest objection is that the first step may already be clear; maybe the real issue comes later. The missing evidence is an observation of where people hesitate and a short question about what they expected to happen next. A safe test could use a prototype and willing participants under an approved research process. We would record what they did, what they said, and what remains uncertain. That last field matters. A few observations can direct the next question; they do not establish a population-wide result. If you have no approved research access, keep the card as a plan. Do not manufacture quotes or silently substitute simulated people for participants. The dashboard case in the book helps us see how a named trade can make evidence relevant. Our exercise turns that lesson into an action you can take without pretending that the answer is already known. Pause and make your own card. Write the decision in a sentence. Write the answer you currently believe. Write the strongest fair objection. Then write one piece of evidence that could change the decision and a safe way to seek it. If your evidence is already available, record its source and date. If it is missing, say missing. Your file should now show a line from priority choice to evidence gap. That line is the point of these first three lessons. A good question can save you from a month of defending the wrong artifact. When you resume, look at the person behind the evidence. We tend to summarize that person as a persona and leave the slide untouched for a year. In the next lesson we will make the customer situation more specific and the persona easier to revise.
You do not have to win the room with a perfect story today. You need a decision that another person can understand, an objection you have taken seriously, and evidence you would actually listen to.
Keep the card attached to your priority page. We are going to use it again.

windows.text: We are back at the Q3 Innovation Plan. The page is no longer empty. You have chosen a priority and written down the evidence that could change your mind. But the broad idea is still sitting there: improve the member experience. Maybe your version says transform onboarding, reinvent support, or use AI to personalize everything. Those ambitions can be useful.

They are hard to test as a single bet. Chapter Five of Accelerated opens with an empty planning document and asks us to think big while building small. The first move is to shrink the question. Instead of “What should we build for everyone?” ask, “What is one moment we can understand better this week?” In our fictional membership service, that moment is the first task after someone joins. A small prototype can show us whether the instruction helps a person begin. It cannot prove the whole program works. That is fine. The point of a small test is to let reality correct the plan before the plan becomes expensive. Now picture the persona deck beside that plan. It looks finished. windows.text: The comments keep coming. One person says the service is slow. Another says it is hard to start. Someone wants a reminder. The inbox is full, and the roadmap meeting is tomorrow. You can count the comments. You can paste them into a summary tool. Neither action tells you what to change.

In Chapter Seven of Accelerated, discovery begins by asking what job people are trying to do when the trouble appears. That means keeping the original words close enough to check our interpretation. Imagine six notes from a membership service. Each has an ID, a moment, and a short comment. We can practice the method with them before applying it to interviews. The decision in our file is whether to improve the first task, add reminders, or investigate another barrier. Before grouping anything, write that decision above the notes. It gives the analysis a purpose. Then ask what evidence would make one of those paths more sensible than the others. A theme is useful only when it helps answer a real choice. The Signals plate is a map of that movement. We start with what people said, examine the situation behind it, and carry a narrower question into the next test. Look at the first two notes. F zero one says, “I clicked begin and could not tell if anything happened.” F zero two says, “I came back later and could not find where I left off.” Both can sound like a request for speed. Their moments are different. The first person needs confirmation that an action worked. The second needs a reliable place to resume. If we label both “performance,” we may build the wrong fix. Give each row an input ID, the exact comment, the task underway, and a proposed job statement. Leave the job statement open to correction. We have not asked a person what they meant. The ID matters because a colleague can return to the note and challenge our reading. Add F zero three, who says the instructions are too long, and F zero four, who says a staff member explained the task in one sentence. Those notes may point to an instruction problem. They may also reflect different circumstances. Chapter Seven uses case structuring to move from anecdote to decision insight. Structuring is not sanding away the detail. It is a way to compare situations without losing the path back to the evidence. If a summary drops the IDs, the team loses that path. Keep the source beside every interpretation.

The book has a useful warning here. In the “Just Make It Faster” case, a team received feedback that sounded like one performance complaint. When they examined the moment behind it, they found different needs: immediate confirmation after an action, current information from other people, and easier movement between views.

The response to one need would not solve the others. I am treating that as a case from the book, not as a measurement of any tool we are showing today. In our example, F zero one belongs under confirmation. F zero two belongs under resume. F zero three and F zero four may belong under instruction clarity. Keep those groups provisional. Now read F zero five: “The first task loaded quickly, but I did not know whether it mattered.” That is a counterexample to the easy “speed” label and a clue about purpose. If we ignored it, we could make a fast page that still leaves someone stranded. F zero six says, “I started after the welcome email showed the first step.” That may support a clearer entry point, but one note cannot establish a general pattern. Ask what the people were trying to accomplish and where the workflow made that harder. The answer should lead toward a question the team can actually test. Suppose a safe local draft groups F zero one through F zero five under “slow onboarding.” It sounds confident. Look at F zero five again. The page loaded quickly. The person did not understand why the task mattered. The draft has collapsed a meaning problem into a timing problem. Move that row back and record why. A tool can help sort a large set, suggest job statements, or point to questions the team has missed. In the book, that is an accelerator for discovery. Chapter Seven calls that danger feedback theater. The correction we just made is small, but it changes the possible product choice. Then write a pattern in cautious language and name the decision it could affect. Resume when someone else could trace your recommendation back to the input rows and see where you might be wrong. None of those six notes proves a solution. They do give us a reason to ask a better roadmap question. Chapter Eight says to turn features into bets about customer and business outcomes. A bet states what we believe will change, for whom, and how we will know. For the membership service, write: “If a clearer first-task card helps new members understand the next action, more of them should begin that task without staff translating the instruction.” That is a hypothesis, not a promise. The other two cards stay on the wall. We need a reason to choose now and a signal that would bring an alternative back. The roadmap should carry both, in words the team can remember. The first-task guide has a plausible connection to our ledger and a small test path. A reminder may help people return, but our six notes do not yet show that forgetting is the main barrier. We are testing one card, and we will observe the starting moment.” Good. Then ask what happens if the member presses begin and loses connection. Does the interface say the action worked? A rising activity line did not answer the question we were trying to solve. Chapter Twelve tells a version of this failure: a dashboard looked healthy while the product was missing the customer outcome. The point is to choose a measure that belongs to the decision.

In the membership service example, the business may care about sustained participation. A member cares about getting started without confusion. The team can first observe whether a person identifies and begins the intended action. Those are different levels of the metrics ladder in the book: business value, customer value, and near-term traction. The lower step does not automatically cause the upper one. We need to test the connection. If page opens rise while people still ask staff what to do, the green chart is a warning, not a win. It also needs a definition that another person can apply to the same event. We will put that definition into the learning plan before seeing any result. Define a successful start before the test begins. For a moderated session, that might mean the participant can point to the intended action, explain its purpose in their own words, and begin without staff explaining the instruction. The numerator is the number of observed participants who meet that definition. The denominator is the number of eligible participants who reach the first-task moment. Record exclusions before the session, such as an interrupted test or a technical outage. A second observer should be able to check the same notes and understand the count. That measure is close to the behavior we seek. It still cannot tell us everything. Ask the participant where they hesitated and what they expected to happen. That qualitative note may show whether the copy, confirmation, or task itself is the problem. Chapter Twelve also warns about destructive metric pairs. We could maximize time spent on the first task while saying we want people to begin quickly. Longer time might mean careful engagement, or it might mean confusion. We need the context before celebrating either direction. Pair the successful-start measure with a guardrail: the person should not have to ask staff to rescue the flow or repeat an action because the state is unclear. Chapter Thirteen gives the learning plan ten components. The first five establish what we are testing. One: business problem and customer outcome. Our example names the friction at the first task and the member's need to begin with confidence. We will not claim a business lift from this small exercise.

Two: target persona or cohort. Use the living persona card from lesson four: a new member at the first-task moment. Add the source and the uncertainty so the card stays honest about what we know. windows.text: You bring a careful recommendation into the room. The research is sound. The test plan has a measure and a stop condition. Someone asks about a competing priority. Engineering asks whose work will move. A person who was not in the meeting raises a concern afterward. The answer becomes, “Let's revisit this next quarter.” Chapter Fourteen opens with a version of that slow no.

Its lesson is practical: the evidence may be strong while the path to a decision is weak. People in the room have different information, responsibilities, and memories of the last failed bet. A leader may see budget risk. An engineer may see a promised platform change. A support lead may see another workflow they will have to explain. Before you call those reactions resistance, find out what each person is trying to protect. Return to the learning plan you wrote in lesson eight. You know the customer behavior you hope to change, the test you propose, and what would stop it. Now write the actual decision you need from this room. Is it permission to run the small test, funding for a larger build, or agreement to stop something else? Those are different asks. For our fictional membership service, the ask is a bounded test of a clearer first-task card. We will map the people and conversations that would make that test responsible. Chapter Fourteen names a Strategic Argument Blueprint. It has six parts, and the order matters. First, the problem: new members struggle to identify the first action without staff translation. That is a hypothesis for this exercise, not a measured customer finding. Second, the opportunity: a clearer entry might reduce that burden and help members begin. We do not assign a revenue figure to that possibility. Third, options: clarify the card, test a guided introduction, or hold the current flow until we learn more. Fourth, the recommendation: test the smallest card change because it gives us an answer with limited build effort. Fifth, tradeoffs: somebody must prepare the card, observe sessions, and delay another small task. Put that cost in the open. Sixth, outcome: the learning plan defines what a successful start looks like and what confusion would stop expansion. This is an argument for a decision, not a list of features. The same six fields can fit a short brief. In an email, lead with the decision requested. In a live meeting, let people see the problem and then the options. In a one-to-one conversation, listen for a missing criterion before polishing the deck. The blueprint does not guarantee agreement. It makes the choice and its cost visible enough for people to challenge honestly.

Chapter Fifteen says an org chart is a start, but it will not show every decision path. Its first stakeholder lens is role type. A decision-maker can approve or stop the work. An influencer shapes that person's view. A gatekeeper controls access, capacity, or information. A champion advocates. A skeptic asks hard questions.

A blocker may actively oppose the idea. One person can occupy more than one role, and the label is a working hypothesis, not a verdict on character. On the synthetic card, a service director can authorize the test. An operations lead controls the staff time needed to observe it. A front-line worker knows where members lose the thread. A finance partner wants to know what the test displaces. We use fictional roles because this exercise needs a map, not anyone's private contact history. Add behavior next. Who tends to ask for customer evidence? Who trusts the team that must build the change? Who remembers an earlier rollout that increased support work? The answer changes what you bring into a conversation. It should not change the underlying evidence. Give the operations lead the observation burden and exclusions. Give the service director the decision and stop condition. Ask the front-line worker whether our assumed friction even matches what they see. If they say no, revise the hypothesis before the meeting. Mapping makes you more accurate about the work and the people who carry it. The book's third lens is a power-interest grid. High power and high interest means manage closely. High power and low interest means keep satisfied. Low power and high interest means keep informed. Low power and low interest means monitor. Those are the book's four labels. Draw the two axes and place our four fictional roles for this one decision. The service director has authority and cares about the member experience, so manage closely. The operations lead can withhold observation time and has a strong interest in the workflow, so manage closely too. The front-line worker may have little formal power but deep interest and useful evidence: keep informed and invite their challenge early. The finance partner may have approval influence but only intermittent interest: keep satisfied with a clear cost and review point. This placement is provisional. A policy change could move finance into the center. A staff member who has the director's trust may carry more informal influence than their title suggests. Ask the people involved, then update the map. Do not use the grid to silence people with less formal power. They may know the customer burden first. The visual helps plan communication; it does not decide whose knowledge counts. Put an objection beside each role and one piece of evidence or question that would help. If you cannot name what would change a person's mind, have a conversation before sending a finished pitch.

The book calls the pre-meeting work Shuttle Diplomacy. Learn the decision criteria before a deck hardens around one answer. Start with the person who will do the observation. Ask the operations lead what time the test would take and which staffing constraint would make it unsafe.

Next, ask the front-line worker whether the proposed card addresses the moment they see members hesitate. If the answer is another problem entirely, record it. Then ask the finance partner what cost or displaced work they would expect to see in the brief. Finally, give the service director the revised options and the specific decision requested. These are conversations with real stakes in a real project. Here they are a fictional sequence for practice, not a report that outreach happened. Keep confidential notes out of a rehearsal tool. If you rehearse objections with AI, use a synthetic brief and treat the output as questions to examine, never as that person's opinion. Chapter Fourteen recommends rehearsing pushback. The stronger version of that advice is to let people correct your understanding when you can speak with them. Update the decision file after each conversation: concern raised, evidence supporting it, what remains unknown, and whether the proposal changed. A meeting can focus on the live choice instead of surprising people with costs that were visible all week. Pause here and use four fictional role names for the decision you have carried through this course. Mark who can decide, who controls resources, who knows the customer situation, and who may challenge the proposal. Put each on the book's power-interest grid. Write their likely interest and objection as a question, because you have not heard their answer yet. Choose one source of evidence or one conversation that could answer each question. Then order the conversations. Who must be heard before the brief is final? Who needs the options and tradeoffs early? Who will make the formal decision? Resume when the map includes the actual decision you seek, four roles, their provisional grid positions, their questions, and a pre-meeting sequence. Keep private names and messages in your authorized workspace. Use fictional roles for this exercise. Look at the six fields of the Strategic Argument Blueprint beside your map. The problem and recommendation may stay the same, but a real objection can change the options, timing, or tradeoff. That is useful learning.

A map is not a way to manufacture agreement. It helps you find missing information and name the people who bear the cost. In the next lesson, we will take the same choice into a short, responsible pitch.
It must tell the truth about what we know, what we hope to learn, and what we would give up to run the test.

windows.text: In Chapter Seventeen, Sam arrives at a roadmap meeting that feels different. The team has already gathered feedback, translated it into a question, and prepared a learning choice. The meeting can spend its time on the decision. Sam is a character in the book's story, not a member of a team we are showing live. What changed was the work before the meeting.

Evidence had a place to arrive. A plan had a review point. A failed test could be discussed without scrambling to explain it away. Think about your last meeting that started with everyone retelling the same customer problem. How much time went into finding the latest notes? How much into arguing over which number was current? Shorter meetings are not the goal by themselves. The useful change is that the team can see what it knows, what it tried, and what it will decide next. Your decision file already holds a source ledger, a learning plan, and a map of the decision room. Today we connect those pages. We will ask where a signal enters, who checks it, how a test is chosen, who decides, and where the result is kept for the next person. That is the quiet infrastructure behind the changed meeting. The book gives Sam a test that fails. The team's learning plan had already said what result would make them change course, so the failure did not have to become a debate about whether the work counted. They could ask what the result meant and choose the next question. Notice what that requires. The original hypothesis must still be visible. The trigger cannot be rewritten after the result. Someone must inspect the evidence rather than accept a summary alone. The decision and its reason need to survive the meeting. In our membership exercise, imagine the new first-task card is tested and people still ask staff for help. That is a conditional branch, not a result. The team might learn that the instruction is unclear, or that the task itself is unfamiliar. The observation notes would need to distinguish those explanations. If participants understand the card but cannot tell whether the action worked, confirmation becomes the next test. If recruitment fails, the study is inconclusive. The file should preserve all three routes without pretending that one happened. Sam's story shows an operating habit: a team can be wrong about a solution and still be disciplined about learning. The record is what lets the next meeting start beyond the last one.

Chapter Eighteen moves from scattered tools to a connected system. Its arrow sequence begins with signal, then insight, test, decision, and repeatable momentum. A signal is a traceable observation, such as a set of first-task notes with source IDs. An insight is an interpretation: perhaps members cannot tell which action starts the service.

That interpretation still needs a counterexample and a person willing to challenge it. A test turns the interpretation into a question that can be answered. The learning plan specifies who participates, what counts, and when the result is reviewed. A decision says what the team will do in light of that evidence. Repeatable momentum means the next person can find the record and use it without rebuilding the whole argument. In our synthetic workflow, feedback note F04 reaches the ledger. The reviewer groups it with similar notes, preserves the contrary case, and writes a proposed job. The owner chooses a small card test. The result, when one exists, returns to the decision file with a date and next move. This path is still a proposal until a team names its owners and review gates. Draw each arrow only after naming its input, owner, and output. A line between boxes is not a handoff unless someone can tell when the work crosses it and what happens when it does not. The book names tools that can collect, translate, and route information. The trap is to connect them and call the system complete. If an AI summary misreads a member's sentence, faster routing only spreads the mistake. In this course, automation may move an approved note into a ledger, flag a possible pattern, or remind an owner that a review date has arrived. A person checks the raw source, contrary evidence, privacy boundary, and decision consequence before a proposed insight becomes a team commitment. That review gate needs a named owner and a visible way to reject or correct the suggestion. For the fictional membership service, a coordinator could review the source IDs before the pattern reaches the product owner. If the note contains private information, it stays in the protected research system and only an approved summary travels onward. The book's minimum viable stack is about connecting the work, not collecting every tool on a shelf. Choose the smallest path your team can actually maintain. Write what happens when the reviewer is unavailable. Does the item wait, move to another authorized owner, or expire? A silent automated approval would change the decision boundary. The loop should make that boundary plain enough for a new teammate to follow.

Imagine joining this work six weeks later. You should be able to answer three questions without searching through a long chat. What did the team believe? What did it observe? What did it decide? The record needs the original hypothesis, the test version, the source links, the measure and guardrail, the reviewer, the decision date, and the next owner.

If the evidence is inconclusive, write that plainly. If a later team repeats the test in a different setting, it should keep the earlier result rather than overwrite it. Chapter Eighteen calls the real goal a system that remembers. Memory here is operational: it keeps a small decision from becoming a rumor. Sam's changed meeting in Chapter Seventeen depends on this kind of continuity. In our exercise, a record might say the first-task card remains untested because observation capacity was unavailable. That is not a failure dressed up as success. It is a clear state and a next action. Another possible record could say the test ran but the result is awaiting human review. windows.text: The feedback pile is growing again. One note says, “I could not tell where to start.” Another asks for a reminder. A third says the task looked complete but the page gave no confirmation. These are fictional member comments carried forward from our earlier exercise. If we group them too quickly under “improve onboarding,” we lose the difference between finding an action, remembering it, and knowing it worked.

Chapter Nineteen introduces ClientQ as a way to translate messy feedback into jobs. The book case gives us a method for examining the notes. The useful discipline is to keep every proposed job tied to the source note that suggested it. Start with what the person was trying to do, the context in which it mattered, and the outcome they wanted. Then ask whether another note points to the same job or a different one. A cluster can be convenient and still be wrong. We also need the contrary note that challenges the pattern. In the decision file, F01 through F06 remain visible beside any synthesis. If one sentence is ambiguous, mark it for a human follow-up rather than turn it into an invented certainty. Today we will write a job card and then test its weak spots with simulation. The source stays visible throughout. Chapter Nineteen makes a crucial distinction: ClientQ processes data; it does not create the underlying customer experience. Work through one fictional note. F01 says the member does not know which action begins the service. The context is the first visit after joining. A possible job is: “Help me identify the first useful action when I arrive, so I can begin without asking staff to translate the page.” That sentence is our interpretation of the note, not a verbatim customer quote. Write F01 beside it. F03 may support the same job, but inspect its wording before adding it. A note about missing confirmation may instead become a separate job: “Help me know whether the action succeeded so I can move on with confidence.” Do not combine them just because they occur on the same screen. The book also shows an outcome-style formulation, such as reducing time spent searching when a task is urgent. We can use that grammar without pretending to have measured importance or satisfaction. If an AI assistant suggests a job, compare it against each source. Ask what word in the original note supports the proposed context and outcome. Where support is thin, label the job provisional. The next step is a question for a person or an observation, not a confident backlog priority.

The book calls ClientQ a translator for customer language. It describes clustering comments, extracting jobs, and moving possible opportunities toward a hypothesis backlog. That is a case in the book. Our six-card exercise is separate. The cards in this exercise are imagined member notes, separate from observed research.

A third category would be actual research collected with permission. Keep these three categories apart when you present a job statement. In a real project, preserve the original note, source date, consent and access rules, the interpretation, and who reviewed it. If a team reports frequency, the count must come from the actual source set and its defined unit, such as people or comments. Do not invent a percentage because several cards on a training slide look similar. The book's warning is clear: synthesis cannot replace talking with people. A pattern extracted from comments may help choose which conversation to have next. It cannot tell us by itself whether a proposed screen solves the need. For our decision file, put the job card beside the first-task hypothesis from earlier lessons. Ask whether the hypothesis still matches the job. If the problem is knowing whether an action worked, a clearer first-task invitation may be the wrong test. Correcting the question before building is progress. Chapter Twenty introduces SudoPoll, a book case for synthetic persona reactions. It can suggest objections to a concept, but its output is a simulation. It is not a customer interview, a survey, or a statistically valid preference count. Imagine asking how a new member might respond to two versions of the first-task card. One simulated response says the shorter card is easier to scan but does not explain what happens after the click. Another says the detailed card feels safer but is too much to read at the doorway. Both reactions are invented for this teaching example. They are useful as questions: do real members need a clearer outcome promise, a stronger confirmation, or less text? They are not votes for one design. The book names three limits around emotional nuance, cultural context, and behavioral prediction. Those limits matter especially when the service touches trust or access. A model can draw on patterns it has seen; it cannot stand in for the people the organization serves. Put a visible Simulation label on every generated reaction. Keep the proposed objection beside the exact concept version that produced it. If the model imagines a concern you had not considered, add it to a validation plan. Do not claim that real customers raised it.

The simulation points to two questions, not two answers. First: can an eligible new member explain the first action before beginning it? Second: after acting, can they tell whether it worked? Put each beside a real observation method. The research owner can watch an approved session, ask the person what they expect, and record the observed hesitation.

windows.text: Picture a Monday meeting. The dashboard is flat. Someone says the product needs a pivot, and the room starts naming new features before anyone has agreed what is stuck. Its numbers are intentionally blank because we have observed no customer result for this exercise.

Start with four possible constraints. Is the customer job poorly understood? Is the product hard to use? Does the way people pay conflict with when they receive value? Or is the offer reaching the wrong buyer? Each explanation points to a different test. A flat chart alone cannot distinguish them. Bring forward the job and evidence gap from the last lesson. If the job is unverified, price changes may only make an unclear service cheaper. If the job is clear and people use the service in bursts, the model deserves scrutiny. Write the assumption that would make a model change sensible. Put its source beside it. A useful diagnosis can also rule out the most attractive explanation. Record the rejected explanation and the evidence that weakened it. That line may save the team from revisiting the same argument next month. StratQuest is the name of the book's guided strategy case. The chapter compares usage-based pricing, a seasonal freemium upgrade, and a professional-services hybrid for a subscription problem. Those are its alternatives, not a recommendation for every business. Put the options side by side. Usage-based pricing can align payment with active use, but billing and cash flow become more variable. A free tier can lower the first commitment, but a generous free offer may never lead to the job people will pay to complete. Keep this comparison on one page. If the proposal requires a second system, a new contract, or more staff time, write that requirement in the same row as its promised benefit.

Now the team can learn whether the concept is understood before investing in the full build. Read the concept to someone outside the project. Ask them to explain it back in their own words. The book's collaboration example surfaces questions about differentiation, infrastructure, notifications, and data. We can use that discipline with our fictional concept. A staff operator may ask how pauses are handled. A funder may ask what outcome the team will measure. None of these imagined questions proves what any real person thinks. Each tells us what to check. This is where the story becomes useful: it gives people something precise enough to question. An objection is strongest when it names the exact sentence and the experience behind the concern. Keep that link in the card so the next revision responds to a real question. Pause and complete two pages of the decision file. On the first, show the current model and at least two alternatives. For each, write the customer job it serves, the operating change it demands, the risk, and the evidence still missing. Choose one alternative to test; record why the others wait. Resume when you can name an owner, a review date, and a stop condition without appealing to a simulated vote. If you are using your own work, use public, synthetic, or approved material. Keep private customer and financial records in their authorized systems. The book's named tools have helped us frame the work, but this packet does not establish that those tools are live or that the book's results will recur. The next lesson asks how to carry the same evidence into two different decision rooms.

Bring the chosen option and its unresolved question forward. A future story earns resources when the people who must live with it can understand and challenge it. The sheet can remain incomplete. An empty evidence cell is a request for work, not a failure of presentation.

windows.text: The plan is ready. The evidence ledger is organized. Yet the first person hearing the recommendation asks about delivery cost, while the second asks who benefits. Chapter Twenty-Three calls this the last-mile problem and introduces Persuasive Business Case GPT. That is a book case, not a live demonstration here. Return to the membership-service alternative from Lesson Thirteen. Imagine asking for permission to test a shorter commitment.

One decision owner manages operations. Another represents the people who use the service. They need different openings, but the underlying claim and source record must remain the same. Write the decision in one sentence before adjusting the pitch. Are we asking to run a bounded test, approve a permanent model, or fund a full rollout? A polished argument can blur those requests. State the smallest actual decision. Then check the evidence column. Which facts come from observed behavior? Which costs are estimates? Which reactions were only simulated? We can tailor the order in which we present them. We cannot promote an assumption into a fact because the room prefers certainty. The chapter's dashboard example shows how a business case changes with the audience. It is a story in the book; we will not repeat its outcome figures as current evidence. For our fictional test, the operations pitch begins with the workload: what staff would have to record, when they would review it, and which service promise remains unchanged. The member-facing pitch begins with the experience: how a person would understand the offer, enter it, and leave without a surprise. Both versions point to the same source note and the same unknown. Neither claims that conversion will rise. Put the common evidence strip under both cards. When you rewrite a sentence, compare it line by line against that strip. If the wording becomes stronger than the record, weaken it or seek evidence. This discipline protects trust. People will disagree about which risk matters most. They should not have to wonder whether they heard two versions of the truth. The question for the pitch is simple: what must this particular person decide, and what can the source actually support?

A persuasive pitch must make the cost visible. The shorter-commitment test could require staff training, a clearer cancellation path, and a way to handle pauses. Those are possible operating requirements in our fictional exercise, not measured costs. Put them on the card before the recommendation. Add the option to keep the current model and the option to defer until the job is verified.

Why test now? Because the evidence suggests a particular mismatch worth examining. Why a bounded test? Because the economics and user experience still have open questions. The book's pre-pitch workflow asks for objections before the meeting, when they can still improve the plan. It also identifies a common mistake: asking an assistant to make a weak case sound strong. Do the reverse. Ask which sentence needs a source, which cost is missing, and which stakeholder can block the test for a good reason. Then revise the proposal. If the answer is that the test cannot be run safely or fairly, say so. A decision brief is useful when it helps the group choose, including a decision to wait. A pre-pitch exercise can surface objections before the room does. Give the proposed test and its evidence to a reviewer. Ask them to challenge the weakest assumption, the delivery burden, and the risk of confusing participants. If an AI assistant produces the challenge, label it Simulation on screen. It has not spoken for operations staff or members. Turn each objection into a check with a real owner. Can the team support a pause? Ask the operator who manages enrollment. Does the offer read clearly? Test the wording with an approved participant. Would a funding partner need a different measure? Ask that partner what decision they must make. The book warns that persuasion does not replace the underlying judgment. Keep the response specific. “We have it handled” tells the room nothing. “We will review support tickets after the first cohort and stop if unresolved access questions rise” is a proposed plan that can be inspected. The precise threshold belongs in the learning plan before exposure. Rehearsal is valuable because it sharpens the next human conversation.

Draft the first sixty-second version for the operations owner. Name the decision, the delivery change, the review date, and what would stop the test. Draft the second for the person accountable to members. Name the job, the proposed experience, the consent boundary, and what remains unverified. These are two ways into one decision. Do not write a promise that the evidence cannot carry.

Annotate each claim with the source ID or mark it assumption. Where a source is absent, change the sentence to a question. Read both versions aloud. The first should sound like someone who has considered the work of implementation. The second should sound like someone who respects the burden of trying a new service. Neither should hide a condition in fine print. If the two versions lead listeners to different decisions, the pitch has drifted. Bring them back to the same bounded request. A source-linked brief lets someone disagree with your recommendation while still trusting your account of the facts. Pause here. Put both pitch versions into the decision file. Under each, list the claims, their exact source IDs, and one objection you still need a person to answer. Add the decision requested, the rejected alternative, the cost, the owner, and the review date. Resume when you can answer this question: what observation would make you change your recommendation? If you cannot answer, the argument is still a defense of a preferred story. Keep private deal terms, customer records, and internal conversations inside approved systems; this exercise uses a fictional proposal. Persuasive GPT remains a named book case.

We have created an editorial teaching card, not proof of a deployed tool or a successful pitch. The next lesson asks what happens after one team learns from a test and other teams want to repeat it. Save the source strip.
At scale, the same evidence will need to survive more meetings, more owners, and more chances for its meaning to drift.

windows.text: One small test was useful. A second team asks to run it too. That sounds like progress, and it may be. It also changes the shape of the work. The first team knew the people, the context, and the reason for every field in its learning plan. The second team receives a template and a sentence about success. Context can disappear between those two moments.

Chapter Twenty-Four asks what changes at scale: experiments can collide, metrics can mean different things, and a tool can spread faster than a review practice. Treat the original test from our fictional membership service as a candidate for reuse, not an approved model. What was the job? Which participants were in scope? What did the team observe? Which result is still pending? If the new team serves people with a different access need, the first team's conclusion may not travel. Put the source and exclusion beside the result. Scaling begins with a transfer of judgment. The useful question is whether another team can reproduce the decision boundary, not whether it can copy the screen. Start the scale-readiness checklist with the parts that must travel: definition, owner, evidence, stop condition, and a place to record the next result. At this point, speed can become a source of error. The first team may know that an apparent improvement came from a narrow group, or that a support burden rose after the measurement window. A copied summary loses both facts. Ask the original owner to mark what another team must verify again. Make that conversation part of the handoff, then record the answer so the next team does not rely on hallway memory. The book proposes shared infrastructure: an experiment template, a hypothesis backlog, and a decision log. These are not three new committees. They are ways to keep a test understandable after the original team moves on. Write a one-page record. It names the customer job, hypothesis, eligibility rule, measure, decision threshold, date, and reviewer. Add links to the source ledger and any observed result. Give the next team permission to say its context differs. A common format makes differences easier to see. Chapter Twenty-Four also warns that a central learning team can become a bottleneck. Assign a local owner who can run the test within an agreed boundary, and a cross-team reviewer for conflicts or shared risk. The governance should fit the consequence. A copy change might need a quick review. A change to pricing, access, privacy, or billing needs the people who own those obligations. This is the practical meaning of light governance: enough common language to coordinate, enough local authority to keep learning, and a clear escalation path when the cost of being wrong rises. The record should help work move, not make people prove that they filled every box. Use the template as a doorway into judgment. A reviewer should be able to spot a missing source or conflicting test without reading a novel. Show who has authority to pause work when an access or privacy problem appears. Write the escalation in ordinary language. If nobody can tell who owns the next decision, the process is too vague to protect the people involved. If every minor edit waits for a central committee, it is too heavy to help them.

Chapter Twenty-Four names five scaling mistakes. A central team can become a bottleneck. Documentation can grow so heavy that people stop testing. The organization can fixate on one tool instead of shared learning. Teams can resist a process they did not help shape. And leaders can expand across the whole organization before the first handoff works. Put those five labels on the checklist and test your own proposal against them.

Which one is most likely here? In the fictional membership case, tool fixation could be tempting: the first team has a spreadsheet, so everyone is told to use the same spreadsheet. What matters is whether the second team can understand the hypothesis, measure, and decision. Another tool could carry the same record if it preserves the contract. windows.text: Go back to the decision you wrote on the first page. At the time, it may have been a broad request: improve onboarding, grow revenue, or use AI to move faster. The file now gives that request edges. It names the person served, the evidence that exists, the alternatives considered, the test that could change the choice, and the people who must review it. Chapter Twenty-Six calls for starting with one pain point.

That is the right size for the next week. Look at the Signals, Alignment, and Momentum labels on the approved Accelerated SAM infographic. They describe the path we have practiced: notice a signal, align a choice, and keep the learning available for the next decision. The art is a map, not a claim that your organization has finished the journey. Which question in your file is both important and answerable in seven days? Choose one. If the evidence is too weak for a launch, the next move may be an interview, a source audit, or a prototype test. A smaller honest move is more valuable than a large promise that cannot be checked. Sam appears again in the final chapter. A junior colleague can find a past decision and use it without asking her to reconstruct the whole story. That is a book illustration, not a verified outcome in this course. The learner's file should make a similar handoff possible on a smaller scale. Read it from front to back. The cover sheet states the data boundary. The priority page records the alternatives you passed over. The evidence ledger and living persona show what you know about the job and what remains uncertain. The roadmap and PRD trace keep the test connected to implementation. The ten-component learning plan names the measure and tripwire. The influence map shows who needs which evidence. The strategy and concept cards show a possible future without treating it as fact. The governance pages tell a second team what can travel. If one page contradicts another, fix the record now. The goal is not a beautiful binder. It is a decision another person can understand, challenge, and revisit. Pick the one unresolved question that matters most to the next move.

Write the next action in a sentence that begins with a verb. Interview three approved participants about the first task. Review six source notes with the service owner. Test two versions of a concept with a small, eligible group. The examples are options, not prescriptions, and their numbers are exercise sizes, not customer outcomes. Choose the move that fits your actual permission and capacity. Add a person who owns it.

Add a review date within the next seven days. Decide in advance what evidence you will collect and where it will be stored. Name one observation that would make you revise the idea and one condition that would stop the test. If the work touches sensitive data, pricing, access, or a promise to a customer, bring the authorized owner into the design before acting. A model can help organize the question or draft a card. It cannot grant consent, approve a change, or absorb responsibility for a result. The final chapter's call to start small becomes practical when the small step has a date and a person attached to it. Before you schedule the review, inspect the source labels. An observed note records what a person actually said or did under an approved process. An interpretation states what you think it means. A simulation suggests a question to ask. These three can sit in one decision file, but they cannot be merged into one claim. The same applies to the book's cases. StratQuest, VisionScope, MarketCraft, Persuasive GPT, and Sam's story belong to the book. They offered teaching frames; they do not establish that a tool is deployed here or that a result happened in your organization. If your next action depends on a result you have only imagined, move the action back to validation. If it depends on private records, keep those records in the system that is authorized to hold them. Use public, synthetic, or approved material for this workshop. Good boundaries make learning possible because the team can tell what it is allowed to use, what still needs consent, and what remains a hypothesis. That clarity makes the next decision easier to trust.

Put a short review on the calendar with the owner and anyone whose work or access the test affects. Send the decision question and the source links in advance. At the meeting, open with what happened, including the observations that complicate your preferred story. Compare the result with the threshold you wrote before the test. Record one of four next states: continue, revise, stop, or gather a specific missing piece of evidence.

Leave the outcome field blank until the review. The book's closing image is a system that grows through repeated choices, not a final piece of software to install once. Your first loop may be a page and a calendar reminder. That is enough if the page is honest and the reminder brings people back to a real decision. If the test fails, keep the learning. If it succeeds in one context, state that context before sharing it. A result becomes reusable when its limits travel with it. Give the next owner a record they can read without guessing what you meant. The chapter's One Year From Now passage imagines a large body of feedback, experiments, and decisions. Treat those figures as a possible future in the book, never as a forecast or a result promised by this course. Pause and assemble the file. Put the one-week commitment on top: the decision, next action, owner, evidence to collect, review date, and stop or revision condition. Check that every claim below it carries a source or an uncertainty label. Resume when you can say the action aloud to another person and they can tell what will happen next. You do not need to run every tool named in the book. You do need a way to notice a problem, test a response, preserve the result, and let someone make the next choice with that knowledge.

The final chapter says the system is unfinished. That is a useful ending because real work changes. People change. Conditions change. A decision file should make revision possible without erasing the path that brought you here. Next week, do the one move you wrote down. Then return to the record. What did you observe? What did it change?
Who needs to know? Write the answer, and the next loop begins.
